title: Minimal Cover
description: Compute equivalent minimal dependency covers using singleton right sides, closure-based extraneous-attribute tests and rule-removal checks, with a complete worked derivation.
notes:
## Simplify dependencies without changing their meaning

A minimal cover is a simplified set of functional dependencies equivalent to an original dependency set. Equivalence means both sets imply the same constraints, not merely that both happen to hold in one sample. The goal is to remove unnecessary attributes and dependencies while retaining the original logical consequences. This makes later reasoning and normalization steps easier to inspect.

Review [functional dependency](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/functional-dependency), [closure of attributes](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/closure-of-attributes) and [3NF](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/3nf). Terminology varies: some treatments reserve canonical cover for a presentation with combined right sides, while minimal cover often uses singleton right sides. State the representation convention before comparing two answers.

## Choose a clear working representation

Here each dependency has one determined attribute on the right. A rule A determines B,C is written as A determines B and A determines C. These forms are equivalent by decomposition and union reasoning. Splitting the right side makes removal tests easier because each working rule asserts one determined fact.

This is a representation change, not deletion of one consequence. If a student rewrites A determines B,C as only A determines B, the C consequence has been lost. Conversely, combining singleton rules with the same left side at the end can improve readability without changing their meaning, provided all right-side attributes are retained.

## Start with a small dependency set

Use attributes A,B,C,D and the dependency set consisting of A→B, AB→C, C→D and A→D. These symbols stand for abstract attributes so the exercise focuses on inference rather than guessing business rules. The relation's candidate keys and normal form depend on this complete set and the relation schema.

The AB determinant in AB→C appears wider than necessary. Since A already determines B, starting from A can derive B and then use AB→C to derive C. Therefore B may be extraneous in that determinant. The test is logical derivability, not whether the letter occurs elsewhere in the written set.

## Test an extraneous left-side attribute with closure

To test whether B is unnecessary in AB→C, compute the closure of A under the current dependency set. Begin with A. A→B adds B, so AB→C can now add C. C→D then adds D. Because C is reachable without assuming B as an initial determinant attribute, replacing AB→C with A→C preserves that rule's effect.

This use of the current AB→C rule is valid: A first establishes B through another dependency before satisfying AB. It is not valid simply to assert the removed attribute initially. Write every closure addition and the rule that justifies it. That record distinguishes a genuine implication from accidentally giving yourself the very assumption being tested.

## Remove redundant whole dependencies

After the left-side simplification, the set is A→B, A→C, C→D and A→D. To test whether A→D is redundant, temporarily remove that entire rule and compute the closure of A under the remaining set. A→C followed by C→D still derives D, so the removed rule contributes no additional constraint.

The remaining singleton set is A→B, A→C and C→D. Removing any one of these loses a required consequence. For example, without C→D, the closure of C does not reach D. That verifies nonredundancy locally. A combined presentation A→BC and C→D describes the same final implications under a different notation convention.

## Keep the two removal tests distinct

An extraneous-attribute test asks whether a smaller determinant still implies the required right-side attribute under the applicable rules. A redundant-dependency test removes the candidate rule before checking implication. Leaving the whole candidate rule in a redundancy test would let it prove itself and would falsely label every rule removable.

These procedures are easy to confuse because both use closures. Name the temporary dependency set and starting attribute set explicitly. A line such as closure of A under F without A→D is far more informative than writing D is obvious. Formal bookkeeping is especially valuable when several dependencies have overlapping determinants.

## Recheck equivalence in both directions

The original set must imply every rule in the proposed cover, and the proposed cover must imply every original rule. One-way implication alone can produce a stronger or weaker constraint set. For the example, the cover implies AB→C because A→C remains valid when additional agreement on B is present, and it implies A→D through C.

The original set implies A→C by the closure already traced, while its other retained rules are directly present. This two-direction check confirms that simplification has changed the presentation rather than the permitted data states. Use closure-based implication checks for each required dependency when the answer is not visually obvious.

## Expect more than one valid minimal answer

A dependency set can have several minimal covers. Different valid removal orders can yield different irredundant presentations while preserving the same closure. Minimal does not always mean globally fewest characters or a unique canonical spelling. Compare the logical implications and stated representation, not only the textual order of arrows.

For example, mutually determining attributes can allow different equivalent routes to an additional attribute. Removing one redundant route first can leave another route in the final cover. An assessment should accept an equivalent minimal singleton cover when the task allows it, rather than requiring one arbitrary ordering chosen by the author's calculation.

## Do not confuse minimal cover with candidate key

A minimal cover simplifies the dependency set. A candidate key is a minimal attribute set determining the whole relation. Both use the word minimal but remove different things for different purposes. A relation can have several candidate keys even when one convenient minimal-cover presentation has already been chosen.

For the example relation ABCD, the closure of A includes all attributes, so A is a candidate key under the stated set. That conclusion does not mean the cover should retain only dependencies beginning with A. C→D expresses a constraint on C that must remain even though A determines the entire row.

## Use the cover as input to design reasoning

A simplified cover is useful when constructing dependency-preserving 3NF decompositions. It makes the determinants and determined attributes explicit and reduces redundant work. However, it does not by itself prove that an arbitrary decomposition is lossless or that every resulting relation has the desired normal form. Those properties require their own checks.

It also does not authorize deleting data or changing a shared schema. The dependency set must first describe verified domain rules. A perfectly executed algorithm over an incorrect assumption about course versions or repeated attempts can still lead to a bad design. Keep the model assumptions with the calculation.

## Validate with implication rather than a lucky instance

A small table can show that a dependency is violated, but cannot establish equivalence over every valid relation. Testing a proposed cover only against today's rows may miss a lost constraint because those rows happen to satisfy both formulations. The proof obligation is logical implication over the modeled domain, not a matching row count.

A useful exercise records the initial rules, singleton expansion, each attribute-removal test, each rule-removal test and final two-way equivalence. Then attempt to remove one more item and explain which consequence would disappear. This final failure test demonstrates minimality and gives reviewers a concrete reason to accept the cover rather than trusting a polished final list. If a closure stops short, record the missing attribute explicitly instead of adding a new rule to rescue the proposed answer. The dependency set is the input contract. Changing it silently turns simplification into a different modeling task and makes the apparent proof impossible for another reviewer to reproduce from the stated assumptions.

questions.question_text: What must a minimal cover preserve?
questions.explanation: Equivalent covers describe the same logical constraints on permitted states.

questions.question_text: Which right-side convention is used here?
questions.explanation: Singleton right sides make individual consequence tests explicit.

questions.question_text: How expand A→BC?
questions.explanation: Both determined attributes must remain represented.

questions.question_text: What is tested by removing B from AB→C?
options: Whether B is stored as text
Whether C is a primary key
questions.explanation: The smaller determinant must imply the original right-side value.

questions.question_text: Under A→B and AB→C what does A's closure gain?
questions.explanation: A first derives B, making the AB determinant available.

questions.question_text: Why is A→D redundant given A→C and C→D?
questions.explanation: The remaining path preserves the same consequence.

questions.question_text: What must be removed during a whole-rule redundancy test?
questions.explanation: Otherwise the candidate can trivially prove itself.

questions.question_text: Can a rule prove itself if incorrectly left in its own redundancy test?
questions.explanation: Keeping the candidate defeats the intended independence check.

questions.question_text: What checks cover equivalence?
questions.explanation: One set can imply another without the reverse holding.

questions.question_text: Can multiple different minimal covers be valid?
questions.explanation: Different removal paths can leave equivalent irredundant presentations.

questions.question_text: Does minimal necessarily mean fewest textual characters?
questions.explanation: Minimality concerns removable logical components under the chosen convention.

questions.question_text: What does a candidate key minimize?
options: An attribute set determining the whole relation
questions.explanation: Key minimality and cover minimality are different tasks.

questions.question_text: For A→B A→C C→D over ABCD is A a superkey?
questions.explanation: A's closure reaches every relation attribute.

questions.question_text: Can C→D be dropped merely because A is a key?
questions.explanation: The dependency constrains rows agreeing on C and adds information beyond A's key role.

questions.question_text: What does A→BC plus C→D represent?
options: A proof of every normal form
questions.explanation: Right-side union can combine retained singleton consequences.

questions.question_text: Does a cover alone prove arbitrary decomposition losslessness?
questions.explanation: Lossless reconstruction needs its own formal conditions.

questions.question_text: What is wrong with equivalence testing only on current rows?
options: Accidental sample consistency can hide lost rules
It always causes a syntax error
questions.explanation: The obligation concerns every permitted relation state.

questions.question_text: Why record the starting closure set?
options: To avoid assuming the attribute being tested away
questions.explanation: A valid derivation may add attributes only through justified rules.

questions.question_text: What should happen if any remaining cover rule is removed?
questions.explanation: Irredundancy means no remaining rule can be deleted without changing implications.

questions.question_text: What must precede formal cover computation in a real design?
questions.explanation: Correct inference cannot repair an incorrect model of valid business states.

coding_not_applicable: This topic is a formal dependency-implication calculation. Meaningful exercises trace closures, test extraneous attributes and prove equivalence; row-result SQL over a sample cannot establish a minimal cover for all permitted relations.

original_questions.question_text: Why is CourseID -> InstructorName dropped when reducing the naive FD set G to its minimal cover?
options: Because InstructorName is not a real attribute
Because it is already implied transitively: CourseID -> InstructorID (G3) and InstructorID -> InstructorName (G4) together already establish it
Because CourseID cannot determine text attributes
Because it has more than one attribute on the right-hand side
original_questions.explanation: A minimal cover excludes any FD derivable from the rest of the set; since the two-step chain already implies it, keeping G6 as a separate FD is redundant.

original_questions.question_text: Why does {StudentID, CourseID} -> StudentName (G9) get reduced/removed during minimal cover derivation?
options: Because StudentName is never functionally dependent on anything
Because CourseID is an extraneous attribute on the left-hand side — StudentID alone already determines StudentName, making G9 a duplicate of G1 once reduced
Because composite left-hand sides are always invalid
Because StudentName must be on the left-hand side, not the right
original_questions.explanation: Testing for extraneous LHS attributes shows CourseID contributes nothing here since StudentID alone suffices; after removing the extraneous attribute, G9 collapses into the already-present G1.

original_questions.question_text: Which of the three formal properties must every FD in a minimal cover satisfy regarding its right-hand side?
options: It must reference at least two attributes
It must consist of exactly a single attribute
It must always be a foreign key
It must match the primary key exactly
original_questions.explanation: One of minimal cover's defining conditions is that every FD's right-hand side contains a single attribute — composite right-hand sides must be split into separate single-attribute FDs first.

original_questions.question_text: What does it mean for an FD in a candidate minimal cover to be 'redundant'?
options: It can be removed from the set without changing the overall closure behavior, because it is already implied by the remaining FDs
It has been used more than once in a query
It refers to a column that is nullable
original_questions.explanation: Redundant means derivable — removing it doesn't lose any information because the rest of the FD set already implies it, as shown with G6 and G7.

original_questions.question_text: After fully reducing the naive 9-FD set G, how many FDs remain in the minimal cover for the running example?
options: 6 — the same clean FD set (F1-F6) used throughout this chapter
0, the relation has no functional dependencies
original_questions.explanation: After dropping G6, G7 (redundant/transitively implied) and G9 (extraneous-LHS duplicate of G1), exactly 6 necessary FDs remain — matching F1-F6 from 21.5.

original_questions.question_text: Why must you recompute closures after each removal step when deriving a minimal cover, rather than just visually judging 'this FD looks redundant'?
options: Because visual judgment is always faster and equally correct
Because whether an FD is truly redundant depends on the exact remaining set of FDs, and an incorrect removal changes the closure/meaning of the FD set
Because closures are irrelevant to minimal cover derivation
Because SQL requires closures to be recomputed automatically
original_questions.explanation: Redundancy is a formal property verified by recomputing closures with the FD removed; a mistaken 'looks redundant' judgment could accidentally change what the FD set actually implies.

original_questions.question_text: Why do schema-design algorithms (like 3NF synthesis) require a minimal cover as input rather than an arbitrary FD set?
options: Because arbitrary FD sets are always syntactically invalid
Because redundant or extraneous FDs can cause the algorithm to produce unnecessary extra tables or miss the true underlying dependency structure
Because minimal covers are required by SQL syntax
Because algorithms cannot process composite left-hand sides at all
original_questions.explanation: Feeding redundant/extraneous FDs into a synthesis algorithm can distort its output; a minimal cover ensures the algorithm reasons only about genuinely necessary dependencies.

original_questions.question_text: Can a single relation have more than one valid minimal cover?
options: No, minimal cover is always perfectly unique
Yes — depending on reduction order in more complex FD sets, different but equivalent minimal covers can result, though they all produce the same overall closure behavior
No, because minimal cover only applies to relations with a single candidate key
Yes, but only if the relation violates 1NF
original_questions.explanation: Minimal covers aren't always syntactically unique; different valid reduction paths can yield different-looking but functionally equivalent minimal FD sets.
